attribution.note: Zitron's own words and his own estimate in his newsletter; the $50B plan is cited as background, but the share estimate is his.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense estimate of OpenAI's share of 2026 global AI compute spend. 'I estimate' attributes the figure to him; it is not a hedge. The normalised text leaves out the infrastructure parenthetical, but the contract handles it separately.

contract.note: The plain reading (OpenAI's 2026 budget against a comparable global compute-spend denominator) is ordinary and fair. Since no denominator is named, the result depends on which accounting boundary is used.

evidence.note: Epoch (Sept 2026, before the evaluation date) confirms a budget of about $50B for 2026. That covers the numerator only and does not establish the global share.
Goldman models $765B in AI capex for 2026, covering chips, data centers and power. That is a different spending boundary, so it is not a comparable denominator.
Epoch puts OpenAI's share of operational compute capacity at about 10–15% at end-2025. That is a different metric (a capacity stock) and an earlier period, so it cannot settle the 2026 spend share.

reviews.rationale: The budget part is roughly corroborated. The central claim, a share above 50% of global 2026 AI compute spend, has no comparable denominator in the packet. The capex and capacity figures use different metrics or periods and are context only. The evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Firm 'aren't going to'/'won't' forecast with no deadline ('at some point'). The debt-financing premise is kept as a qualifier. The 65% HBM aside is left ungraded, which is appropriate.

contract.note: Reading the financing premise at industry level and requiring an actual decline in quantities is ordinary and fair. Correctly, continued growth does not refute an undated forecast.

evidence.note: MUFG (Dec 2025) shows hyperscalers turning to debt to fund AI capex. This is evidence of the premise, not of the predicted decline.
S&P (Aug 2026) reports continued debt and other financing of AI infrastructure. This also bears on the premise only; it shows no inability to buy GPUs.
NVIDIA's purchase commitments, mostly for memory, rose sharply by July 2026. So no decline has happened yet, but this cannot refute an eventual one.

reviews.rationale: Firm forecast with no deadline. Evidence confirms the premise that hyperscalers are borrowing, but nothing in the packet documents GPU purchases falling because of financing limits or a resulting drop in NVIDIA's HBM needs. Rising commitments show only that it has not happened yet, which does not count against an undated forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' forecast with no deadline. Correctly, the nearby mention of 2027 is not imported as a deadline.

contract.note: Defining 'run out of money' as exhausting liquidity and failing to pay obligations as they come due is the ordinary reading and fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: SoftBank's own disclosure says it completed its $30B investment on Oct 1, 2026. This is relevant to liquidity, but it neither shows exhaustion nor disproves it.

reviews.rationale: Open-ended forecast, and no documented liquidity failure appears by the cutoff. New funding was completed in October 2026, but continued solvency at any given date cannot contradict 'at some point'. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'All but certain' expresses high confidence, so the no-device part is a scored forecast tied causally to the lawsuit. 'Potentially the company itself' is hedged and correctly left unscored.

contract.note: In context ('its hardware efforts'), 'a device' fairly means the consumer device the lawsuit concerns. A three-year reading of 'few years' is ordinary, though the evaluator supplied it. Whether the Codex Micro counts depends on how 'a device' is read.

evidence.note: Court order confirms Apple's lawsuit was filed July 10, 2026, which establishes the premise. The October order concerns limited discovery only; it does not bar any release.
Ars reports the Codex Micro keypad went on sale July 15, 2026. That is a branded peripheral, not the consumer device the lawsuit concerns.
Fortune says the keypad is separate from the consumer companion device, which is expected next year. An expected release is not a release.
A Feb 2026 report already showed the device slipping to 2027, before the lawsuit. This makes causation harder to attribute but does not settle the outcome.

reviews.rationale: The horizon (read as July 2029) has not arrived. The qualifying consumer device has not been released, and the litigation has not produced any irreversible block on release. The Codex Micro does not count under the fair contextual reading. Nothing conclusive has happened, so the forecast is not yet scored.
